## The model

In the [model with constant technology](index.qmd), GDP per capita stops growing
once the economy reaches its steady state. Here technology grows at a constant
rate $g$, and it enters the production function as the efficiency of labour:
$Y = K^\alpha (AL)^{1-\alpha}$. The term $AL$ is the number of *effective
workers*: if $A$ doubles, each worker can do what two could before. As before,
labour grows at rate $n$, capital depreciates at rate $\delta$ and a constant
fraction $s$ of output, the investment rate, is devoted to capital
accumulation.^[Textbooks usually call $s$ the *saving rate*; see the note on the [first page](index.qmd).]

Capital per worker now grows without limit, so the model is written in terms of
capital per effective worker, $k = K / AL$, which does settle down. Output per
effective worker is $y = k^\alpha$ and capital evolves according to

$$
k_{t+1} = \frac{s k_t^\alpha + (1 - \delta) k_t}{(1 + n)(1 + g)} .
$$

The steady state is

$$
k^* = \left( \frac{s}{\delta + n + g + ng} \right)^{\frac{1}{1 - \alpha}} .
$$

## Simulation

Press play, or drag the time slider, to follow the economy from its initial
capital stock $k_0$. The top row shows the same $k_t$ in both charts: on the left,
the gap between investment and break-even investment is what moves $k$; on the right,
that movement is traced out over time. The remaining charts show GDP per capita,
$Y / L = A k^\alpha$, and the levels of the capital stock, $K = k A L$, and the
labour force, $L$, with $A_0 = L_0 = 1$. These keep growing after $k$ has settled
at its steady state: GDP per capita then grows at the rate of technology, $g$,
shown as a dashed line on the growth chart. On a log scale, constant growth
appears as a straight line.
